content: Assisted mechanical ventilation is a critical intervention for neonates with various respiratory and surgical conditions. However, this life-saving procedure carries potential risks and complications. To mitigate these adverse effects, new suctioning techniques have been introduced into clinical practice. One such technique involves endotracheal suctioning without disconnecting the neonate from the ventilator. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of this closed suctioning method in intubated, ventilated neonates. The review utilized the search strategy of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group and included a comprehensive search of databases such as Cochrane, MEDLINE, and CINAHL, as well as abstracts from the Society for Pediatric Research. The search was completed in July 2011. The review included all trials that used random or quasi-random allocation of patients and compared suctioning with and without disconnection from the ventilator. Standard Cochrane Neonatal Group methods were employed for data collection and analysis. Each reviewer independently assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted data, resolving any discrepancies through discussion. A fixed-effect model was used for analysis, with outcomes reported as relative risk (RR) for categorical data and mean difference (MD) for continuous variables. Four trials involving a total of 252 neonates were included in the review. These trials used a cross-over design to compare suctioning with and without disconnection. The findings demonstrated that suctioning without disconnection significantly reduced episodes of hypoxia, with a relative risk of 0.48 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.31 to 0.74) based on data from three studies involving 241 participants. Additionally, fewer neonates experienced a decrease in transcutaneous partial pressure of oxygen (TcPO2) by more than 10%, with a relative risk of 0.39 (95% CI: 0.19 to 0.82) in one study involving 11 participants. Closed suctioning also resulted in a smaller percentage change in heart rate, with a weighted mean difference of 6.77 (95% CI: 4.01 to 9.52) based on data from four studies involving 239 participants. Furthermore, fewer neonates experienced a heart rate decrease of more than 10%, with a relative risk of 0.61 (95% CI: 0.40 to 0.93) in three studies involving 52 participants. The incidence of bradycardic episodes was also reduced during closed suctioning, with a relative risk of 0.38 (95% CI: 0.15 to 0.92) based on data from three studies involving 241 participants. The authors concluded that there is some evidence suggesting that suctioning without disconnection from the ventilator improves short-term outcomes in neonates. However, the evidence is not robust enough to recommend this technique as the sole method of endotracheal suctioning. Future research involving larger trials is needed to explore the impact of different suctioning techniques on ventilator-associated pneumonia, pulmonary morbidities, and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Additionally, it is essential to include extremely preterm infants (less than 28 weeks of gestation) in these studies to better understand the implications for this vulnerable population.
